## make a simple regression model

```{r}
bears <- read.csv(file="BEARS.csv",header = TRUE)
#adjust factors to be factors
bears$SEX<- as.factor(bears$SEX)
bears$MONTH<- as.factor(bears$MONTH)
```

## Model LENGTH ~ NECK  this is an example  
```{r}
plot(LENGTH~NECK, data=bears, pch=19)
```

This model displays that as the neck circumference increases, the length of the neck also increases at a primarily linear manner. 

```{r}
model.1 <- lm(LENGTH~NECK,data=bears)
summary.lm(model.1)
```

The adjusted R-squared is 0.7476.
    
Compare all models that predict LENGTH other than NECK. Then order them from worst to best by its value of Adjusted-Rsquared (bigger is better), or by RSE (residual standard error) where smaller is better. 

## Model LENGTH ~ HEADLEN
```{r}
plot(LENGTH~HEADLEN, data=bears, pch=19)
```

This model displays that as the head length increases, the length of the neck also increases at a primarily linear manner. 
    
```{r}
model.2 <- lm(LENGTH~HEADLEN,data=bears)
summary.lm(model.2)
```

The adjusted R-squared is 0.8434.

## Model LENGTH ~ HeadWTH
```{r}
plot(LENGTH~HEADWTH, data=bears, pch=19)
```    

This model displays that as the head width increases, the length of the neck also increases at a primarily linear manner.

```{r}
model.3 <- lm(LENGTH~HEADWTH,data=bears)
summary.lm(model.3)
```

The adjusted R-squared is 0.5321.

## Model LENGTH ~ CHEST
```{r}
plot(LENGTH~CHEST, data=bears, pch=19)
```    

This model displays that as the chest increases, the length of the neck also increases at a primarily linear manner.
    
    
```{r}
model.4 <- lm(LENGTH~CHEST,data=bears)
summary.lm(model.4)
```

The adjusted R-squared is 0.7869.

## Model LENGTH ~ WEIGHT
```{r}
plot(LENGTH~WEIGHT, data=bears, pch=19)
```        

This model displays that as the weight increases, the length of the neck also increases at a primarily linear manner.   

    
```{r}
model.5 <- lm(LENGTH~WEIGHT,data=bears)
summary.lm(model.5)
```

The adjusted R-squared is 0.7423.

## Models from WORST to BEST
The worst model was the model of the relationship between the length and the head width that had an adjusted R-squared of 0.5321 and whose plot was linear like but not strongly correlated.
```{r}
plot(LENGTH~HEADWTH, data=bears, pch=19)
```    

The second worst model was the model of the relationship between the length and the weight that had an adjusted R-squared of 0.7423 and whose plot was linear like with a bit of a curve and correlated better than the worst model but was not the best. 
```{r}
plot(LENGTH~WEIGHT, data=bears, pch=19)
```  

The middle model was the model of the relationship between the length and the neck that had an adjusted R-squared of 0.7476 and whose plot was linear and correlated with a middle strength correlation(not the strongest but not weak either).

```{r}
plot(LENGTH~NECK, data=bears, pch=19)
```

The second best model was the model of the relationship between the length and the chest that had an adjusted R-squared of 0.7869 and whose plot was linear and correlated with a stronger correlation.
```{r}
plot(LENGTH~CHEST, data=bears, pch=19)
```

The best model was the model of the relationship between the length and the head length  that had an adjusted R-squared of 0.8434 and whose plot was linear and correlated with a strong correlation.
```{r}
plot(LENGTH~HEADLEN, data=bears, pch=19)
```

Final Standings from Worst to Best: 

Length and Head Width Model 3 - 0.5321

Length and Weight Model 5 - 0.7423

Length and Neck Circumference Model 1 - 0.7476

Length and Chest Model 4 - 0.7869

Length and Head Length Model 2 - 0.8434
